lore_book.magictreasures.couriers_letter:
Dear Mam,

I am a courier now, for the pearl lady up the coast. She gave me silver bands that let me see at night, so I run the coast road in the dark like a fox with lanterns for eyes.

Last night I carried a letter from the druid to the runesmith. It was eleven pages. The runesmith's answer was one line. I waited an hour for it.

I am paid by the letter, not the page. I have raised this with her.

A bat flew into my face at the river ford, and I saw it coming, which was worse.

I am eating well. Do not worry. Tell Pip he cannot have my room.

Your loving son,
Tam
lore_book.magictreasures.ledgers_last_pa:
Last page.

The boy was mine to teach. He is mine to finish.

Forty years of wards, and the best one was never for a door. Closed it into the Orb: every weld I know, folded in on itself.

Found him below the old chapel, among his bones. He didn't fight. Asked if it would hurt. Told him I didn't know.

Shut the crypt. The ward holds while the Orb is whole, and nobody holds the Orb but me.

Can't leave it where his kind could find it. Taking it north, past where Silbro went. Somewhere old enough that nothing digs.

If you're reading this, the forge is cold. The Orb is under the...
lore_book.magictreasures.letters_across_:
Friend,

The willow you laughed at has given me a second ring. The pearl woman's runner brings it, so you may laugh at it in person.

Keep it from the forge. It dislikes fire.

- Silbro

Silbro,

Ring arrived. Laughed. Put it on the anvil and hit it. Hammer bounced.

What did you do to it?

- S. Stone

Nothing. That is the whole of it. I waited, and the tree did the rest.

You hit things until they agree with you. I wait until they agree with me. We both get rings.

- Silbro

Silbro,

Waiting is not a craft.

Sent you a ward for your door. Keeps out fever, thieves and wolves. Does not keep out squirrels. Did not try.

- S. Stone

The squirrels thank you. They are living in it.

It is a fine ward, my friend, the finest closed thing I have ever seen. I only wish you would leave something open now and then.

- Silbro

Silbro,

Open things leak.

Come down for the midsummer fair. Bring the ring. I want to hit it again.

- S.

Friend,

The boy's mother is buried. I sat with her three days and could not keep her. He thanked me at the grave, politely, and did not look at me once.

Watch him.

- Silbro

Silbro,

He's back at the anvil. Works harder than before. Best hands I've had.

Grief is grief. Leave him be.

- S. Stone

A fox came to my door, alive and hollow as a scraped gourd. Something drew it empty and let it walk away.

I have only met one person who asked me how a thing could be emptied.

- Silbro

Silbro,

Foxes get sick.

The boy has no one but this forge. I won't turn him out on a druid's feeling.

- S. Stone

They say in the market that the mill village on the east road stands empty. They say you made the reeve a ward for his door, and would not take his coin.

Write to me, Stone.

- Silbro

Friend,

A year, and no letter. The runner says the forge is lit, so I know you are alive, and that is all I know.

I will not ask what you knew. Only write.

- Silbro
lore_book.magictreasures.maldritchs_note: Maldritch

Master Stone says magic is set, not made. A hammer closes it into metal like a weld.

I have watched him do it a hundred times and I still cannot see the moment it happens.

I will.

A summer with the druid. Silbro talks to willows and they listen. He let me hold a ring he grew. It was warm.

If a living thing can hold magic, it is already full of it. Why wait to be given?

Mother is sick. The healers' charms do nothing.

Silbro came himself and sat with her three days. He was kind. He was patient.

She died on the fourth.

He said some things cannot be mended, only let go.

I have decided he is wrong.

The gentle way is too slow.

A rabbit. Bone holds nothing; everyone knows that. But I closed a ward around the life as it left, the way Master Stone closes a weld, and the bone kept it.

It was warm, like the willow ring.

I have told no one. Master Stone would not understand. Silbro would understand too well.

I am not doing anything wrong. I am only learning faster.
Maldritch's Notes, I
Maldritch

The rabbit bone held nine days, then went cold. A ward closed at the moment of death keeps what is left, and what is left is very little.

Take it before the end, not at it.

A goat, sedated. I drew from it while it lived, into a ward of thigh bone. The bone held four times what the rabbit gave, and the goat lived a day after.

Living things refill. Silbro was right about that much.

Bone is the right vessel. It was alive once; it remembers being full, and it wants to be again. Silver only holds. Bone pulls.

Master Stone would call that a leak. It is a well.

The belt is finished: small skulls on a band of iron, each one a ward. Worn, it feeds a ring as a spring feeds a pond.

I wore it to the forge. Master Stone did not look at it. Bren did.

Animals are slow. Each holds a little and takes a season to fill again, and the woods near the forge are going quiet.

I need a vessel that holds more, and lives in numbers.

The mill on the east road has forty souls.

I have been counting.
Maldritch's Notes, II
Maldritch

The village held more than I needed. I carry it in the belt, and the belt carries me.

Master Stone has put me out of the forge. He did not shout. I think I would have preferred it.

Bone outlasts flesh. So I have closed my life into my own bones, the way I closed the rabbit's, only slowly, and from the inside.

It did not hurt. Nothing hurts now.

The children in the next valley ran from me. I have made a mask, so that the living see a man when they look.

It is a good likeness. I used to look like that.

They made a ring once, the three of them: Stone's blood-metal, the druid's living heart, the pearl woman's dust in the ruby. I took it to undo what I am. To die again.

It will not let me die. It will not stop drinking.

I remember being afraid. I don't remember why.

Stone is coming. I can feel his wards closing, one by one, like doors down a long hall.

Let him come.
Maldritch's Notes, III
BY ORDER OF THE REEVE

The mill village on the east road stands empty. No sickness was found there, and no raiders seen. Its folk lie in their beds as if asleep, and they are cold.

Buy no charms of bone. Trade with no pale young smith who sells them, nor give him lodging. If he is seen, send word to the reeve, and to Master Stone at the forge.

Do not hold what he offers. It is warm.
A Warning, Posted in the Market
lore_book.magictreasures.selenes_account:
They will tell you there were three: the runesmith, the druid, and the one we don't name in harbours.

There were four. I sold the other three their pearls, and I am the one still here to write it down.

Sal'andaar thought magic was a thing you hammered shut. Silbro thought it was a thing you were given.

They argued for forty years and were both right, which neither of them could stand.

Pearls are grown, you know. An oyster takes a grain of grit, a wound, and wraps it in light, year after year.

Silbro understood at once. Sal'andaar asked what the oyster charged.

I made bands for my couriers, so they could run the coast roads by night and see the ruts before they fell in them.

Half the letters between the runesmith and the druid went by my runners. I read none of them. Mostly.

And the boy. Maldritch. Clever hands, frightened eyes. He asked me once how long a pearl lives.

I told him: longer than the oyster.

I have wondered since if that was the worst thing I ever said.

I have kept their papers, what I could find. Read them as you find them.

You will not find them all. I have seen to that.

- S. T.
lore_book.magictreasures.selenes_last_pa:
I am the last. A pearl does not age while the sea keeps it, and the sea has kept me longer than I asked.

Silbro is a wood now. Stone went north with his Orb and did not come back. The boy is where Stone left him.

I gathered what they wrote. Most of it is harmless: a druid's seasons, a smith's accounts, the letters of two stubborn old friends.

The boy's notes are not. Read in order, they are a recipe.

So I have scattered them, one book to a chest, from here to the far coast.

If you ever hold them all, burn the boy's. Keep the letters. They were the best of us.

- S. T.
lore_book.magictreasures.silbros_journal: Silbro

Spring.

The smiths in the valley laughed when I told them wood could hold magic. They are right, in their way. Dead wood cannot. Cut a branch and the magic runs out of it like sap.

So I did not cut the willow by the mill. I sat with it instead, and asked.

A tree answers slowly. It took the whole of that first summer before I felt it lean toward my hand.

Second summer.

A root has curled around my finger while I slept. I have not moved it. It is warm, which roots are not meant to be, and when I set a little healing into it, the healing stayed.

Third summer.

The ring is grown. It holds mana as well as any silver ring I have seen at the forge, and when I cracked it on a stone it mended itself, once.

I do not think it will do that twice.

I showed it to Sal'andaar. He turned it over for a long time and said only, "Show me how."

I told him the truth: you cannot make it. You can only wait to be given it.

He did not like that answer.

It is a little pleased with itself, I think.

So am I.

- S.
Silbro's Journal, I
Silbro

Autumn.

Hale the woodcutter came up the hill with his arm in a sling. Thirty years of the axe, and the elbow gave out before he did.

I did not mend the arm. I asked the oak he cuts to help him.

The bracers took the winter: oak bark, still on the tree when I began, grown around a band of willow.

He swings as he did at twenty. He says he can hear the oak in them when he works. I expect he can.

Spring.

The village healer asked for something she could carry. I gave her a token cut from a living elm, no bigger than a thumbnail.

It does not heal. It only reminds the hurt that they can.

Summer.

Sal'andaar has sent me his best apprentice, "to learn patience." His name is Maldritch. Quick hands, quick eyes, and a sadness he wears like a cloak in August.

He listens to the willows better than I did at his age. I let him hold the ring. He held it a long while.

Then he asked me how it could be emptied. Not filled. Emptied.

I told him a ring is not a cup. What it holds was given, and given things are not taken back.

He nodded as if he understood. I do not think he believed me. He goes home tomorrow.

- S.
Silbro's Journal, II
Silbro

Autumn, and I am old.

Stone has written at last. Three lines. The boy is gone from the forge; he does not say where, and I do not ask. I have had his silence long enough to read it.

The oldest wood I know is two days north. It has been calling me since spring, the way the willow did, only slower, and much deeper.

I think it is my turn to be given to something.

I leave the willow's ring on the sill, for whoever needs it. Not for whoever wants it. It will know the difference; it always has.

Tell Stone I was right about waiting. Tell him kindly.

[The last lines are not written. They are pressed into the page, like the grain of wood.]

roots are slow

they are not lonely

go gently
Silbro's Journal, III
lore_book.magictreasures.smiths_ledger.p:
Ledger of S. Stone, runesmith.

Three horseshoes, a mended plough. 4 copper.

A ward set in a farmer's ring, against fevers. 1 silver. He paid in eggs. Wrote it down as a silver anyway.

Took on two apprentices.

Bren: strong, slow, honest.

Maldritch: best hands I've had. Learns a weld in a day that took me a year.

Asks too much about the dead.

Silbro sent another ring that grew itself. Sent him back a horseshoe that didn't.

He'll know what I meant.

The coat is done. Took the winter. Spells slide off it like rain off oilcloth.

Tested it on myself. Then on Maldritch, at his asking. He laughed the whole time.

Should not have let him.

Maldritch gone three days. Came back with a bone charm that holds mana.

Bone doesn't hold mana. I know what does, and so does he.

We did not speak of it.

Bren has left. Says he won't work beside "that one".

Orders are down. Folk in the market cross the street.

The ward for the reeve's door: no charge.
lore_book.magictreasures.tidewalkers_log:
Spring tide, full moon.

Pearls brought up: eleven. Good ones: two. The oysters keep their own counsel.

Noted again: the dive is easier under a full moon. The sea gives back what you spend in it.

Neap tide.

Ran out of light on the coast road and put the cart in a ditch. Lost a wheel and a temper.

Must make the couriers something better than lanterns.

New moon.

The bands are done: plain silver, a sliver of pearl set inside each, against the skin. Worn at night, the road shows grey instead of black.

The couriers call them journeyman's bands. I let them.

Spring tide again.

Stone asks why my pieces cost less to work by night. I told him the moon pulls the sea, the sea pulls the pearl, and the pearl pulls whatever is set around it.

He wrote that down.

High water.

Swam out past the bar at dusk to check the beds, and came back with more in me than I took out. I am forty years older than my couriers, and I swim the way they run.

I have stopped asking why.
